Appendix B Effective Lagrangian to Scattering Form Factor

EXCEED-DM can compute DM-electron scattering rates that can be written in terms of the transition matrix elements in Eqs. (11) - (16). The main theoretical problem is then going from a UV Lagrangian to the scattering form factor, ℱI​F\mathscr{F}_{IF}, used in Eq. (18). At a high level, this is done in two steps: first, find the non-relativistic limit (NR) of the UV Lagrangian (see Refs. [34, 39] for a more detailed discussion of this step). Second, from the NR effective Lagrangian, use Fermi’s Golden rule to compute the scattering rate, and reference cross section, and then manipulate the resulting formula to the form used in Eq. (18). The first step is well outside the scope of this paper. In this appendix we will focus on the second step, starting from a fairly generic NR effective Lagrangian, and deriving the scattering form factor directly in terms of the operators appearing in the NR effective Lagrangian. To illustrate the usefulness of this approach we will derive the scattering form factors for the two models focused on in the main text: the kinetically mixed dark photon model, Secs. IV.1, IV.4, and the ‘V-A’ DM model in Sec. IV.2.

Our starting point is the NR effective Lagrangian of a DM fermion, χ\chi, coupling to the electron, ψ\psi,

ℒeffNR⊃χ†​ψ†​𝒪​χ​ψ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\text{NR}}_{\text{eff}}\supset\chi^{\dagger}\psi^{\dagger}\mathbf{\mathscr{O}}\chi\psi (53)

where ψ,χ\psi,\chi are the two component NR electron and DM fields, respectively, and 𝒪\mathscr{O} is the interaction operator. χ\chi and ψ\psi each have units of eV3/2\text{eV}^{3/2}, and 𝒪\mathscr{O} has units of eV−2\text{eV}^{-2}. Assume an incoming DM particle with momentum 𝐩\mathbf{p} and spin ss scatters off an electronic state |I⟩|I\rangle, creating to an outgoing DM particle with momentum, 𝐩′=𝐩−𝐪\mathbf{p}^{\prime}=\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q} (qq is the momentum transferred to the target) and a final electronic state |F⟩|F\rangle. Fermi’s Golden Rule tells us that the transition rate due to the Lagrangian in Eq. (53) is given by,

ΓI,𝐩,s→F,s′=2​πV​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​δ​(EF−EI−ω𝐪)​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪s​s′|I⟩|2,\displaystyle\Gamma_{I,\mathbf{p},s\rightarrow F,s^{\prime}}=\frac{2\pi}{V}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\delta(E_{F}-E_{I}-\omega_{\mathbf{q}})|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}\,, (54)

where EIE_{I}, EFE_{F} are the energies of the electronic states, ω𝐪=𝐪⋅𝐯−q22​mχ\omega_{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{v}-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}, 𝐯\mathbf{v} is the incoming DM velocity, and mχm_{\chi} is the DM mass. The volume, VV, and exponential factor come from the incoming and outgoing DM states, χ|𝐩,s⟩=V−1/2ei​𝐩⋅𝐱ξs\chi|\mathbf{p},s\rangle=V^{-1/2}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\xi_{s}, and ξ↑=(10)\xi_{\uparrow}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, ξ↓=(01)\xi_{\downarrow}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}. 𝒪s​s′\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}} is simply the s,s′s,s^{\prime} component of 𝒪\mathcal{O} in Eq. (53), i.e., 𝒪s​s′=ξs′†​𝒪​ξs\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}=\xi_{s^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\mathscr{O}\xi_{s}.

Assuming the DM is unpolarized we spin average (sum) over the initial (final) DM spin states in Eq. (54) to get the spin average interaction rate,

ΓI,𝐩→F=2​πV​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​δ​(EF−EI−ω𝐪)​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪s​s′|I⟩|2¯,\displaystyle\Gamma_{I,\mathbf{p}\rightarrow F}=\frac{2\pi}{V}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\delta(E_{F}-E_{I}-\omega_{\mathbf{q}})\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}}\,, (55)

where the overline notation indicates (1/2)∑s​s′(1/2)\sum_{ss^{\prime}}. Assuming the DM velocity distribution is given by fχ​(𝐯)f_{\chi}(\mathbf{v}) and g⁡(𝐪,ω)≡2​π​∫d3​𝐯​fχ​(𝐯)​δ​(ω−ω𝐪)g(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv 2\pi\int d^{3}\mathbf{v}f_{\chi}(\mathbf{v})\delta(\omega-\omega_{\mathbf{q}}), the average transition rate between two electronic states becomes,

ΓI→F=1V​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​g​(𝐪,EF−EI)​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪s​s′|I⟩|2¯.\displaystyle\Gamma_{I\rightarrow F}=\frac{1}{V}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}g(\mathbf{q},E_{F}-E_{I})\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}}\,. (56)

The transition rate per kg-year, RR, is then simply this interaction rate multiplied by the number of DM particles in the target, divided by the target mass, and summed over initial and final states,

R=ρχmχ​ρT​V​∑I​F∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​g​(𝐪,EF−EI)​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪s​s′|I⟩|2¯,\displaystyle R=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}\rho_{T}V}\sum_{IF}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}g(\mathbf{q},E_{F}-E_{I})\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}}\,, (57)

where ρχ\rho_{\chi} is the DM density, and ρT\rho_{T} is the target density. Eq. (57) is most useful if one is interested in finding the rate as a function of the Lagrangian parameters in the NR EFT since it is directly related to the 𝒪\mathscr{O} appearing in Eq. (53). However, it is useful, and common practice, to write this rate in terms of a reference cross section, which is simply a function of the underlying Lagrangian parameters. In terms of 𝒪\mathscr{O}, the reference cross section is given by,

σ¯e≡μχ​e24​π​∑s​s′,σ​σ′|𝒪s​s′,σ​σ′|2,\displaystyle\bar{\sigma}_{e}\equiv\frac{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}{4\pi}\sum_{ss^{\prime},\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}|\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime},\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}|^{2}\,, (58)

where μχ​e\mu_{\chi e} is the DM, electron reduced mass. This function is evaluated at reference momentum scales, e.g., q=q0=α​meq=q_{0}=\alpha m_{e}, and ignores screening effects, ε=1\varepsilon=1. We can now write Eq. (57) in terms of the reference cross section. At the risk of abusing notation, we define,

𝒪^s​s′=𝒪s​s′14​∑s​s′,σ​σ′|𝒪s​s′​σ​σ′|2,\displaystyle\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}=\frac{\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\sum_{ss^{\prime},\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}|\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime}\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}|^{2}}}\,, (59)

and the rate can be written as,

R=π​ρχ​σ¯eμχ​e2​mχ​ρT​V​∑I​F∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​g​(𝐪,EF−EI)​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪^s​s′|I⟩|2¯.\displaystyle R=\frac{\pi\rho_{\chi}\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}m_{\chi}\rho_{T}V}\sum_{IF}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}g(\mathbf{q},E_{F}-E_{I})\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}}\,. (60)

From here, the connection to Eq. (18) is a simple rearrangement, and we see that the scattering form factor is simply |⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪^s​s′|I⟩|2¯\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}} with the propagator dependence factored out,

ℱI​F=1fscr2​ℱmed2​|⟨F|ei​𝐪⋅𝐱​𝒪^s​s′|I⟩|2¯.\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{IF}=\frac{1}{f_{\text{scr}}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{\text{med}}^{2}}\overline{|\langle F|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}|I\rangle|^{2}}\,. (61)

With Eq. (61) we can compute the scattering form factor for the dark photon and ‘VA’ DM model. We begin with the dark photon model which has the UV Lagrangian,

ℒ⊃gχ​Vμ​χ¯​γμ​χ+ge​Vμ​e¯​γμ​e,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset g_{\chi}V_{\mu}\bar{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\chi+g_{e}V_{\mu}\bar{e}\gamma^{\mu}e\,, (62)

where VμV_{\mu} is the dark photon and it has standard kinetic terms. If the coupling geg_{e} is due to kinetic mixing, then ge=e​κg_{e}=e\kappa, where κ\kappa is the kinetic mixing parameter. It can be shown that the NR EFT Lagrangian and 𝒪\mathscr{O}, are,

ℒeffNR\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{eff}}^{\text{NR}} ⊃ge​gχε⁡(q,ω)​(q2+mV2)​χ†​ψ†​ψ​χ\displaystyle\supset\frac{g_{e}g_{\chi}}{\varepsilon(q,\omega)\left(q^{2}+m_{V}^{2}\right)}\chi^{\dagger}\psi^{\dagger}\psi\chi (63)
𝒪s​s′,σ​σ′\displaystyle\mathscr{O}_{ss^{\prime},\sigma\sigma^{\prime}} =ge​gχε⁡(q,ω)​(q2+mV2)​δs​s′​δσ​σ′,\displaystyle=\frac{g_{e}g_{\chi}}{\varepsilon(q,\omega)\left(q^{2}+m_{V}^{2}\right)}\delta_{ss^{\prime}}\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\,, (64)

for a material with an isotropic dielectric function, where mVm_{V} is the dark photon mass, and ω\omega is the energy transferred to the target. We will find the scattering form factor in two limits, for a heavy and light dark photon. We begin by computing 𝒪^s​s′\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}},

𝒪^s​s′=δs​s′​1ε⁡(q,ω)​{q02q2light1heavy.\displaystyle\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}=\delta_{ss^{\prime}}\frac{1}{\varepsilon(q,\omega)}\begin{cases}\frac{q_{0}^{2}}{q^{2}}&\text{light}\\ 1&\text{heavy}\end{cases}\,. (65)

In both cases, fscr=1/εf_{\text{scr}}=1/\varepsilon, and ℱmed\mathcal{F}_{\text{med}} takes its standard form for heavy and light mediators. The scattering form factor is the same in both the light and heavy dark photon models,

ℱI​F=|𝒯1|2.\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{IF}=|\mathcal{T}_{1}|^{2}\,. (66)

Moving on to the VA DM model we follow the same steps, first by writing down the UV Lagrangian,

ℒ⊃gχ​Vμ​χ¯​γμ​χ+ge​Vμ​e¯​γμ​γ5​e.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset g_{\chi}V_{\mu}\bar{\chi}\gamma^{\mu}\chi+g_{e}V_{\mu}\bar{e}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{5}e\,. (67)

Following Ref. [34, 23] after taking the NR limit of the currents and integrating out the dark photon, the NR effective Lagrangian is,

ℒeffNR⊃gχ​geq2+mV2​χ†​ψ†​[𝐊e⋅𝝈e2​me−𝐊χ⋅𝝈e2​mχ+i​𝝈e⋅(𝐪×𝝈χ)2​mχ]​ψ​χ,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{eff}}^{\text{NR}}\supset\frac{g_{\chi}g_{e}}{q^{2}+m_{V}^{2}}\,\chi^{\dagger}\psi^{\dagger}\left[\frac{\mathbf{K}_{e}\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{e}}{2m_{e}}-\frac{\mathbf{K}_{\chi}\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{e}}{2m_{\chi}}+\frac{i\bm{\sigma}_{e}\cdot\left(\mathbf{q}\times\bm{\sigma}_{\chi}\right)}{2m_{\chi}}\right]\psi\chi\,, (68)

where 𝐊e=2​𝐤e+𝐪\mathbf{K}_{e}=2\mathbf{k}_{e}+\mathbf{q}, 𝐤e\mathbf{k}_{e} is the electron momentum, 𝐊χ=2​𝐤χ−𝐪\mathbf{K}_{\chi}=2\mathbf{k}_{\chi}-\mathbf{q}, 𝐤χ\mathbf{k}_{\chi} is the DM momentum, and σχ\sigma_{\chi} (σe\sigma_{e}) are the Pauli matrices acting in DM (electron) space. Contrary to the kinetically mixed dark photon model, there is no screening. Since the dark photon couples to electrons via the spin operator, 𝝈e\bm{\sigma}_{e}, there is no mixing between the dark photon-photon to generate screening terms.

The NR effective Lagrangian in Eq. (68) can be further simplified since the last two terms are of order 𝒪⁡(vχ)\mathcal{O}(v_{\chi}), whereas the first term is 𝒪⁡(ve)\mathcal{O}(v_{e}). Since ve∼α∼10−2v_{e}\sim\alpha\sim 10^{-2} the first term will dominate and we will approximate the interaction with just the first term. Therefore,

𝒪^s​s′=ℱmed​𝐊e⋅𝝈eKe0​δs​s′\displaystyle\hat{\mathscr{O}}_{ss^{\prime}}=\mathcal{F}_{\text{med}}\frac{\mathbf{K}_{e}\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{e}}{K_{e}^{0}}\delta_{ss^{\prime}} (69)

where Ke0K_{e}^{0} is some reference momentum, which we take to be α​me\alpha m_{e}. Therefore the scattering form factor is,

ℱI​F=1(α​me)2​[4​me2​|𝒯𝐯⋅𝝈|2+2​me​𝒯𝐯⋅𝝈​(𝐪⋅𝒯𝝈)∗+2​me​𝒯𝐯⋅𝝈∗​(𝐪⋅𝒯𝝈)+|𝐪⋅𝒯𝝈|2].\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{IF}=\frac{1}{(\alpha m_{e})^{2}}\left[4m_{e}^{2}\left|\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\bm{\sigma}}\right|^{2}+2m_{e}\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\bm{\sigma}}\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\bm{\sigma}}\right)^{*}+2m_{e}\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\bm{\sigma}}^{*}\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\bm{\sigma}}\right)+|\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\bm{\sigma}}|^{2}\right]\,. (70)

This scattering form factor can be further simplified for targets which have spin degenerate eigenstates, since the electron spin sum can be performed analytically. Performing the electron spin sum, (1/2)∑σ​σ′(1/2)\sum_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}, gives,

ℱI​F=1(α​me)2​[4​me2​|𝒯𝐯|2+2​me​(𝐪⋅𝒯𝐯)​𝒯1∗+2​me​(𝐪⋅𝒯𝐯∗)​𝒯1+q2​|𝒯1|2].\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{IF}=\frac{1}{(\alpha m_{e})^{2}}\left[4m_{e}^{2}\left|\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}}\right|^{2}+2m_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}}\right)\mathcal{T}_{1}^{*}+2m_{e}\left(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{v}}^{*}\right)\mathcal{T}_{1}+q^{2}|\mathcal{T}_{1}|^{2}\right]\,. (71)

where I,FI,F are now just the band labels.

Appendix C Transition Matrix Elements for Bloch States

We will discuss the explicit derivation of the transition matrix elements, ⟨I|𝒪|F⟩\langle I|\mathcal{O}|F\rangle for the Bloch states discussed in Sec. II.1. Note that since bloch_PW_basis, bloch_STO_basis, bloch_single_PW are simply different bases of the same approximation, these formula hold for all them. We begin with an insertion of the identity, 1=(1/V)∑s∫d3𝐱|𝐱,s⟩⟨𝐱,s|1=(1/V)\sum_{s}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x},s\rangle\langle\mathbf{x},s|, where VV is the target volume,

𝒯i,f,𝐤,𝐤′=1V​∑s∫d3​𝐱​ei⁡(𝐪−𝐤′)⋅𝐱​uf,𝐤′,s∗​(𝐱)​⟨𝐱,s​|𝒪^|​I⟩,\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{i,f,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{s}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}\,e^{i(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\cdot\mathbf{x}}u_{f,\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\langle\mathbf{x},s|\hat{\mathcal{O}}|I\rangle\,, (72)

where 𝒪^\hat{\mathcal{O}} is an operator inside the 𝒯\mathcal{T}’s in Eqs. (11) - (16) without the ei​𝐪⋅𝐱e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{x}} term. All of these 𝒪^\hat{\mathcal{O}} are diagonal in momentum space, therefore it is simplest to insert a momentum space identity,

⟨𝐱,s​|𝒪^|​I⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{x},s|\hat{\mathcal{O}}|I\rangle =V∑s′∫d3​𝐩(2​π)3ei​𝐩⋅𝐱𝒪s​s′(𝐩)⟨𝐩,s′|I⟩.\displaystyle=V\sum_{s^{\prime}}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{O}_{ss^{\prime}}(\mathbf{p})\langle\mathbf{p},s^{\prime}|I\rangle\,. (73)

One can further show that,

⟨𝐩,s|I⟩=1V∑𝐆,s′u~i,𝐤,s′,𝐆δ3(𝐤+𝐆−𝐩),\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{p},s|I\rangle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{G},s^{\prime}}\widetilde{u}_{i,\mathbf{k},s^{\prime},\mathbf{G}}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{p})\,, (74)

and therefore

⟨𝐱,s​|𝒪^|​I⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{x},s|\hat{\mathcal{O}}|I\rangle ≡ei​𝐤⋅𝐱​[𝒪^⋅u]i,𝐤,s=ei​𝐤⋅𝐱​∑𝐆,s𝒪s,s′​(𝐤+𝐆)​u~i,𝐤,s′,𝐆​ei​𝐆⋅𝐱,\displaystyle\equiv e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\left[\hat{\mathcal{O}}\cdot u\right]_{i,\mathbf{k},s}=e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\sum_{\mathbf{G},s}\mathcal{O}_{s,s^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\widetilde{u}_{i,\mathbf{k},s^{\prime},\mathbf{G}}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\,, (75)

where we have introduced some convenient shorthand notation []\left[\right] for application of the operator in Fourier space, and 𝒪s​s′​(𝐩)≡⟨𝐩,s​|𝒪^|​𝐩,s′⟩\mathcal{O}_{ss^{\prime}}(\mathbf{p})\equiv\langle\mathbf{p},s|\hat{\mathcal{O}}|\mathbf{p},s^{\prime}\rangle.1212 12 In words, the procedure to compute [𝒪⋅u]\left[\mathcal{O}\cdot u\right] is compute uu, Fourier transform it to find u~\widetilde{u}, apply the 𝒪\mathcal{O} operator in momentum space, then Fourier transform back.

Substituting Eq. (75) in to Eq. (72), and using the periodicity of uu, then gives,

𝒯i,f,𝐤𝐤′\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{i,f,\mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}} =1V​∑s∫d3​𝐱​ei⁡(𝐪−𝐤′+𝐤)⋅𝐱​uf,𝐤′,s∗​[𝒪⋅u]i,𝐤,s\displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{s}\int d^{3}\mathbf{x}e^{i(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{x}}u^{*}_{f,\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s}\left[\mathcal{O}\cdot u\right]_{i,\mathbf{k},s} (76)
=∑𝐆δ𝐪,𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆​1Ω​∑s∫UCd3​𝐱​ei​𝐆⋅𝐱​uf,𝐤′,s∗​[𝒪⋅u]i,𝐤,s\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}\delta_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}}\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{s}\int_{\text{UC}}d^{3}\mathbf{x}\,e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{x}}u^{*}_{f,\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s}\left[\mathcal{O}\cdot u\right]_{i,\mathbf{k},s} (77)

where UC indicates a sum of the unit cell. Note that, as a result of crystal lattice momentum conservation, 𝒯\mathcal{T} only has support at the kinematically allowed points, 𝐪=𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}. Alternatively we can simplify this as,

𝒯i,f,𝐤,𝐤′​(𝐪=𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{i,f,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}) =1Ω​∑s∫UCd3​𝐱​ei​𝐆⋅𝐱​uf,𝐤′,s∗​[𝒪⋅u]i,𝐤,s,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{s}\int_{\text{UC}}d^{3}\mathbf{x}\,e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{x}}u^{*}_{f,\mathbf{k}^{\prime},s}\left[\mathcal{O}\cdot u\right]_{i,\mathbf{k},s}\,, (78)

which is the transition matrix element that gets computed for every pair of crystal electronic states.
